header:
Date: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dina Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Maya Chen (CTO, PioneerAI), Jordan Lee (Platform Eng, PioneerAI), Ravi Singh (ML Eng, PioneerAI)
Recording: yes
Notes: Discovery focused on migrating from OpenAI-hosted to Redwood Dedicated/Private, compatibility with vLLM/TGI, evaluation parity, cost/latency tradeoffs.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Rivera (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 50 minutes, we'll do a quick intro and then dig into your migration questions from OpenAI into a Dedicated or Private setup.
[00:12] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): Thanks Alex, appreciate it. We're trying to get off OpenAI for a bunch of reasons — costs, control, and data residency. Curious what Dedicated looks like, and if we can keep the eval parity with what we run today.
[00:28] Alex Rivera (Redwood): Totally. I'll hand over to Samir in a bit for the deep technical stuff, but at a high level Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, predictable throughput, and you can lock model versions. Private options give you VPC/on-prem control and KMS integrations.
[00:43] Jordan Lee (PioneerAI): Quick question — we run most inference via the OpenAI API with a mix of their gpt-4o for chat and a couple smaller models for routing tasks. We're also experimenting with vLLM and TGI on our infra for cost-sensitive stuff. How compatible is Redwood with those runtimes and our current prompts?
[01:02] Samir Patel (Redwood): Great question. Redwood's serving runtime supports a wide range of model formats and we do compatibility work for vLLM/TGI exported weights. For prompts, in most cases you get eval parity but a few things to watch: tokenization differences if you switch tokenizers, and generation hyperparams — Redwood allows you to control temperature, top-p, max_tokens, stop sequences similarly to OpenAI.
[01:22] Ravi Singh (PioneerAI): When you say tokenization differences, do you mean subtle changes that could affect our ranking evals? We have a strict QA pipeline where a small BLEU/ROUGE change triggers rollback.
[01:34] Samir Patel (Redwood): Yes — small. Usually the same base tokenizer will be used, but sometimes model conversions use different BPE merges or byte pair handling; we keep an eye on that. We recommend exporting a tokenization map from your current provider and we can run a token-level diff. Also we do eval parity tests: you give us your prompt set and we run the same sequences to compare outputs and metric deltas.
[01:56] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): That sounds good — we can share our eval set. How long does the parity testing take?
[02:03] Samir Patel (Redwood): For a standard prompt set of a few thousand prompts, expect 48–72 hours to run at dedicated test capacity, depending on model size. We also do a head-to-head latency/cost comparison.
[02:15] Alex Rivera (Redwood): On the commercial side, Dedicated is usage plus a reserved capacity commitment; we can tailor the pool size to match your 95th percentile throughput. For many customers the tipping point is if you have sustained heavy usage — that's where Dedicated reduces unit cost and gives you SLOs.
[02:33] Jordan Lee (PioneerAI): Our monthly token volume is roughly 1.2B tokens now and spiky during peak product hours. We need sub-200ms tail latency for chat and cheaper batch for embeddings. Can Redwood do mixed latency/cost routing?
[02:48] Samir Patel (Redwood): Yes — smart routing is a Redwood core feature. You can define policies to route critical low-latency requests to dedicated low-mdp instances with higher cost, and lower-priority batch to cheaper quantized variants or to burst capacity. The runtime automatically falls back if dedicated capacity is exhausted.
[03:05] Ravi Singh (PioneerAI): About model variants — we use gpt-4o and some open LLMs. Will you host the same model weights, or do we move to Redwood-verified variants?
[03:16] Samir Patel (Redwood): We have a model catalog. For proprietary models you can bring your weights to Dedicated/Private. For OpenAI models, the common pattern is to shift to a comparable open model we host or you host on dedicated hardware. We also support customer-supplied checkpoints for Private deployments. We provide performance/quality profiles per model so you can pick.
[03:36] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): We can't bring OpenAI weights — obviously — but we've been fine with some open models in experiments. Our main concern is eval parity: can your hosted variants match our current outputs closely enough?
[03:47] Samir Patel (Redwood): Often yes, sometimes with small adjustments. We run alignment/finetune steps where necessary, and can recommend quantization/compilation profiles that maintain quality. If needed, we can do a short finetune job on your prompts and small in-domain dataset to close gaps.
[04:06] Jordan Lee (PioneerAI): Security is critical. We need SOC2, audit logs, SSO, KMS for key control, and optional on-prem. What does Redwood provide?
[04:16] Dina Ortiz (Redwood CSM): We have SOC 2 Type II, support SAML/SSO, RBAC in the console, audit logs, and KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments. For Dedicated we provide network isolation and per-customer encryption at rest. We can share the security pack after the call.
[04:31] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): Great, please send. Also we need to know about data retention and PII handling — how long data is kept, can we disable logging?
[04:41] Dina Ortiz (Redwood CSM): You control retention policies. You can disable persistent transcript storage for sensitive routes, and we provide redaction hooks. For Private on-prem deployments you keep all logs locally.
[04:52] Alex Rivera (Redwood): Back to compatibility — you mentioned vLLM/TGI on your infra; are you using them for lower-cost batch or as part of a canary?
[05:01] Ravi Singh (PioneerAI): Both. We run TGI for fast turnaround in some tasks and vLLM on GPU pools for higher concurrency. We want to centralize but keep the ability to run cheaper variants locally.
[05:12] Samir Patel (Redwood): Redwood supports hybrid setups. You can use Redwood for production-critical paths and keep vLLM/TGI for local dev/batch. We can help with artifact conversion; many customers use our caching and KV-cache semantics to replicate warm-start performance they had with vLLM.
[05:28] Jordan Lee (PioneerAI): Anything tricky about the KV cache transition? We use aggressive prefix caching to shave off tokens.
[05:35] Samir Patel (Redwood): The KV cache semantics are similar; main consideration is serialized KV format differences between runtimes. We'll provide a migration adapter and recommend a cache invalidation strategy. When we move to Dedicated, the runtime preserves per-session KV where appropriate and offers cache metrics in Console.
[05:51] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): On the ops side, how do we manage versions and rollouts? We need canary + automatic fallback to OpenAI in case of regressions during cutover.
[06:02] Samir Patel (Redwood): Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies. You define success criteria (latency, error rate, eval metric) and if thresholds fail the system auto-rolls back to the previous model or provider. We also integrate with SLO/alerting tools.
[06:19] Ravi Singh (PioneerAI): For the initial POC, what do you recommend we test? Prompt set, latency/load, and cost comparison? Anything else?
[06:28] Samir Patel (Redwood): Exactly. We recommend: 1) Eval parity suite, 2) Load tests to simulate peak traffic and tail latency, 3) Cost model runs for your traffic shape, and 4) Security compliance checklist. We can run a POC on small Dedicated slice to gather metrics.
[06:43] Alex Rivera (Redwood): Commercially we usually propose a month-long POC with reserved capacity and a success checklist. If it looks good, we move to a committed Dedicated plan. For Private, timelines depend on network and infra — 4–8 weeks typical for VPC, longer on-prem.
[06:58] Jordan Lee (PioneerAI): Sounds reasonable. On pricing, do you provide unit cost per token or per-inference? We bill both ways internally.
[07:06] Alex Rivera (Redwood): We can present both. Dedicated typically reduces per-token cost via reserved GPU amortization; we show modeled cost per inference based on your token distribution. We'll send a pricing deck.
[07:16] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): One more technical — we use function-calling patterns with structured JSON outputs. Will Redwood's runtime preserve that and support streaming?
[07:26] Samir Patel (Redwood): Yes, function/tool calling and structured outputs are supported, including streaming responses. We also have structured validation hooks you can plug in to enforce response schemas.
[07:37] Ravi Singh (PioneerAI): Regarding model compilation and quantization — we saw artifacts where aggressive int8 quantization reduced quality. Do you have recommended profiles per model?
[07:47] Samir Patel (Redwood): We do. Our Optimize team maintains recommended quantization profiles and kernel selections for each model/sequence length. For POC we'll run a few quantization profiles to find the best cost/quality tradeoff and show delta metrics.
[07:59] Jordan Lee (PioneerAI): For the future, could we burst to Redwood Hosted if we run out of Dedicated capacity? Some of our peaks are unpredictable.
[08:08] Alex Rivera (Redwood): Yes — hybrid routing to Hosted or even fallback to other regions/providers is supported. We can set cost caps and fallback policies.
[08:17] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): Any red flags so far from your side? Limits we should know before committing?
[08:25] Samir Patel (Redwood): Mostly operational: plan for data transfer time to replicate prompt history if you use large context; plan capacity for KV warm-up. For Private deployments, network egress and firewall config can add lead time. Other than that, nothing blocking.
[08:39] Alex Rivera (Redwood): Let's go through a quick recap and next steps.
[08:43] Alex Rivera (Redwood): Action items: Alex will send pricing and Dedicated sizing options; Samir will share a compatibility checklist and migration guides; PioneerAI to share eval set and current OpenAI usage. We'll schedule a technical deep dive next week.
[08:57] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): We'll get the eval set and billing export over. Can you also include a sample security pack and SOC2 docs?
[09:04] Dina Ortiz (Redwood CSM): Yes, we'll attach the security pack and our compliance docs.
[09:09] Jordan Lee (PioneerAI): For the technical deep dive, can Samir include a demo of the KV cache and a sample canary rollout?
[09:16] Samir Patel (Redwood): Absolutely, will prepare a short demo and a migration checklist.
[09:21] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): One quick follow-up: we use a mix of private prompts and customer data in chat. If we go Private on-prem, what's the recommended way to handle secrets and KMS?
[09:31] Dina Ortiz (Redwood CSM): For Private on-prem, you can integrate your KMS/HSM. We support customer-managed keys and can map entitlements so no keys leave your environment. For Dedicated, we offer KMS integration with key rotation policies.
[09:44] Ravi Singh (PioneerAI): On monitoring — do you expose per-route token costs and latency histograms?
[09:49] Samir Patel (Redwood): Yes, Console has per-route cost, latency percentiles (P50/P95/P99), token breakdowns, and tracing hooks. We can also forward metrics to your Prometheus/Grafana.
[10:02] Alex Rivera (Redwood): Great. Unless there are more questions, we'll wrap and get the materials out.
[10:08] Maya Chen (PioneerAI): No more questions — thanks everyone. We'll look for the pricing and the security pack.
[10:14] Alex Rivera (Redwood): Thanks, Maya and team. Talk soon.
[10:19] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: speaker overlaps and some transcription artifacts present; product names occasionally mis-transcribed (e.g., 'v-L-M' vs 'vLLM').
